Introduction

Seeing wind turbines across northern China made me wonder whether they are usually far from where people live. I studied this question in Inner Mongolia, Heilongjiang, Jilin, and Liaoning.

My first-order spatial hypothesis was that turbine locations would have lower population density and greater distance to urban centres than random locations in the same region. I studied where turbines are located, not whether they change an area’s future development.

Data and Methods

I combined turbine records from COWTD with WorldPop population data, GHSL urban centre boundaries, and geoBoundaries provincial boundaries.

I selected turbines first observed by 2020 to match the population and urban data. Of 20,128 candidate records, 635 fell outside the selected regional boundaries. I retained 19,493 turbines and used the boundary polygons to assign them to regions.

For each turbine, I calculated population density in its raster cell and the shortest distance to an urban centre polygon. A turbine inside an urban centre has a distance of zero. Nearby urban centres outside the study region were also considered.

I ran 999 Monte Carlo simulations per region, keeping the same number of points as observed turbines. Points were sampled uniformly by area within each region, restricted to valid population coverage. I compared population-density and urban-distance medians, using two-sided tests and a Holm adjustment for the eight comparisons.

Are Turbines More Remote?

The results differed by region.

  • Inner Mongolia and Heilongjiang: turbine locations had higher population density and were closer to urban centres than the simulated baseline.
  • Jilin and Liaoning: turbine locations had lower population density and were slightly farther from urban centres.

The clearest contrast was in Inner Mongolia. Its observed median urban distance was 61.4 km, compared with 90.6 km under the simulated baseline. Although the turbines looked remote, they were closer to urban centres than typical random locations in the region.

All eight Holm-adjusted p-values were 0.016 under this baseline. However, the urban-distance differences in Jilin and Liaoning were only about 1.44 km and 2.08 km. A statistically significant difference is not necessarily a large one.

Observed Values and Random Baselines

Triangles show the observed medians. Circles and grey intervals show the simulated medians and their middle 95%. These intervals describe the random baseline, not uncertainty intervals for the observed medians.

Where Are Turbines Concentrated?

I summarized turbine intensity using a 50 km projected grid. Counts were divided by each cell’s actual area inside the study region and expressed as turbines per 1,000 km².

The map shows an uneven distribution, with concentrations in parts of Inner Mongolia and the northeast. The highest-intensity cell contained 1,179 turbines in 2,500 km², or about 472 turbines per 1,000 km². This peak was not caused by a small clipped cell. The map is descriptive, rather than a statistical hotspot test.

A 3D View

Column height and colour show the same turbine intensity as the 2D map. The columns are display symbols, not actual wind-farm footprints. Their heights do not represent terrain or turbine height. Rotate the map and hover over a column to explore its values.

Limitations and Next Steps

My random baseline does not account for wind resources, terrain, land use, or clustering within wind farms. The tests show differences from this baseline, not a complete explanation of turbine locations.

The first-observed year is not necessarily the installation year. Population values describe the turbine’s grid cell, and urban centres do not include every town or village. Selection by original province labels may also omit turbines inside the study region that were labelled as belonging to another province.

A useful next step would be to add wind and terrain data, compare grid sizes, and use simulations that account for wind-farm clustering.

Conclusion

My initial hypothesis was supported in direction in Jilin and Liaoning, but reversed in Inner Mongolia and Heilongjiang. An apparently remote location is not always more remote than its surrounding region. These findings do not show that turbines cause population decline or prevent future development.

Data Sources

  • COWTD: turbine coordinates and first-observed years.
  • WorldPop 2020: UN-adjusted population counts, aggregated to nominal 1 km cells.
  • GHSL Urban Centres 2020, R2023A: urban settlement polygons.
  • geoBoundaries CHN ADM1: provincial boundaries.
